deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the previous page): a 'système de pseudodroites' is a map (cellular decomposition) on the real projective plane X. All vertices have even order >= 4, so edges group into 'pseudolines', and any two pseudolines meet in exactly one point. X~ = S^2 is the orientation double cover, and D~ is the preimage of a pseudoline D.

This page:
(1) Each pseudoline D carries an induced polygonal structure. Its vertices S_D are the points where D meets the other pseudolines, and its edges are the edges of the map lying on D. This structure 'has a clear meaning' when s_D = |S_D| >= 3. The page then restates the previous page: the two components of X~ \ D~ (the 'hemispheres') correspond bijectively to the two orientations of D, and hence to the two orientations of the combinatorial polygon D. The cases s_D = 2 and s_D = 1 are first mentioned, then struck out, and taken up again in the margin.
(2) Let s be a vertex. Exclude the case where all pseudolines pass through s (then s is the only vertex). Then some pseudoline D avoids s. The set Omega_s(X) of local orientations of X at s is in canonical bijection with Omega(D), the orientations of the combinatorial polygon D. Topologically, X \ D is an open disc containing s. Its boundary circle double covers D by an orientation-compatible covering, so an orientation at s gives an orientation of D. Equivalently, s has one lift in each hemisphere of X~ \ D~.
(3) Problem: for two pseudolines D, D' both avoiding s, describe the composite bijection Omega(D) -> Omega_s(X) -> Omega(D') purely in terms of the 1-skeleton K^1 and its decomposition into pseudolines. Let t = D ∩ D'.
- Since s has order >= 4, at least two pseudolines Delta, Delta' pass through s; take them not through t.
- Let u, u' (resp. v, v') be the intersections of Delta (resp. Delta') with D, D'.
- The four pseudolines D, D', Delta, Delta' are in general position. A 4-element pseudoline arrangement in general position is stretchable and combinatorially unique ('position standard').
- So corresponding orientations are those for which the order of (u, v) on the interval D - {t} matches the order of (u', v') on D' - {t}.

The next page generalizes this to k lines Delta_i through s and not t: the bijection is the one making the linear orders of the u_i on D-{t} and of the u'_i on D'-{t} agree. In the real case this is central projection from s. It then treats the degenerate case where only one pseudoline through s avoids t.

Purpose: a purely combinatorial (map-theoretic) reconstruction of the orientation data at vertices. In modern terms this amounts to recovering local or global orientation data (in effect, the chirotope up to sign) of a rank-3 oriented matroid from the cell complex of the arrangement.
errors: The main text suggests s_D >= 3 is needed for the polygon structure to make sense. But s_D = 2 occurs: for three pseudolines in general position, each one carries exactly 2 vertices. s_D = 1 occurs exactly when all pseudolines are concurrent. A 2-gon (2 vertices, 2 distinct edges) still has two well-defined combinatorial orientations; only s_D = 1 (a loop) is genuinely degenerate. Grothendieck seems aware of this: he strikes out '(Si s_D = 2 ou s_D = 1' and adds a marginal note about the cases '=1 ou ...'.

The bijection Omega_s(X) ≅ Omega(D) is asserted without proof. It is correct: the complement of a pseudoline in RP^2 is an open disc, and the double cover of D by its boundary is orientation-compatible.
The procedure needs two pseudolines through s that avoid t. This can fail: for example, only one line through s may avoid t. That case is deferred to the next page.
The appeal to 'position standard' for 4 lines in general position is correct but unproved here. It is the easy small case of stretchability.

ideas.what: Pseudoline arrangement defined as a map on RP^2 with even vertex degrees and pairwise single intersection; each pseudoline gets an induced polygon structure.
ideas.modern_name: Projective pseudoline arrangement / its cell complex (rank-3 oriented matroid via Folkman–Lawrence)

ideas.what: Local orientations at a vertex s correspond to orientations of any pseudoline avoiding s (complement of a pseudoline is a disc / hemisphere picture in the double cover S^2).
ideas.modern_name: Orientation double cover; the affine chart RP^2 minus a line; the 'line at infinity' and the induced orientation

ideas.what: Combinatorial description of the comparison bijection Omega(D) -> Omega(D') via lines through s cutting D and D'. Orders of the cut points on D-{t} and D'-{t} must correspond (central projection from s); uses uniqueness and stretchability of 4 lines in general position.
ideas.modern_name: Perspectivity / central projection; consistency of local orientations (chirotope signs) in rank-3 oriented matroids
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical projective geometry; oriented matroid theory (Bland–Las Vergnas, Folkman–Lawrence, Björner et al.)

deep.surprise_reason: This is careful but elementary groundwork: recovering orientation data combinatorially from a pseudoline arrangement. It is essentially standard in oriented matroid theory (the 1970s–80s) and classical projective geometry. The only interest is the historical one: Grothendieck developing this theory independently, in his map ('carte') language, around 1981.
transcription_corrections: '(cela a un sens clair, voir l'ens. S_D de ces sommets est ≥ 3)' should read roughly '(cela a un sens clair si l'ens. S_D de ses sommets est ≥ 3)'.
'Soit s un sommet de la cart[?]' should read 'Soit s un sommet de la carte'.
'non concourantes avec D, D'; mais u, u' ...' should read '... non concourantes avec D, D'; soient u, u' (resp. v, v') les int. de Δ (resp. Δ') avec D, D''.
'dont l'int. est distinguée par s' should read 'dont l'int. est désignée par t', i.e. t := D ∩ D'. 'Non concourantes avec D, D'' thus means 'not passing through t'.

Marginal diagonal note is only partly legible: 'Il vaut peut-être mieux noter Ω_D ... (orientations de) la structure de polygone ... ' with a case distinction 's_D = 1 ou ≥ ...'. It apparently repairs the s_D ≥ 3 restriction.
'61' at the bottom is the archive folio number, not mathematics.
